title: The Dirty Truth: The Clean Energy Revolution Is a Mirage
author: Chris Keefer
target_audience: General readers interested in energy and climate change
Students studying environmental science or public policy
core_themes: The limitations and challenges of renewable energy sources
Critique of the narrative around clean energy solutions
Examination of the environmental impacts of different energy sources
Advocacy for nuclear energy as a solution to climate change
primary_purpose: To challenge mainstream assumptions about renewable energy, expose what the author sees as the pitfalls and shortcomings of the current clean energy narrative, and argue for the inclusion of nuclear power as an essential, realistic component of future energy systems.

structure_format.narrative_style: Investigative and polemical, with technical explanations and real-world examples
structure_format.organization: Chapters devoted to dissecting various forms of energy (solar, wind, hydro, nuclear), policy frameworks, and case studies from around the globe
features: Personal anecdotes from the author’s experience
References to recent reports and academic studies

key_concepts_lessons: Renewable energy sources like wind and solar have inherent limitations and cannot alone meet global energy needs reliably.
There are significant environmental, economic, and practical obstacles to a purely renewables-based energy transition.
Nuclear energy is often misunderstood; its risks are frequently exaggerated compared to its proven safety and efficiency.
The public discourse on energy is rife with misinformation which influences political and investment decisions.
Clean, reliable, and abundant energy is essential for human prosperity and climate mitigation.
notable_features: Highlights real-world energy usage data and limitations
Balances environmental concerns with practical realities
Advocates a controversial stance in mainstream environmental debates
cultural_historical_context: Published amid intensifying debates over global energy transition pathways and climate policy, particularly after COP26 and subsequent energy crises, the book arrives at a time when many governments are investing heavily in renewable technologies and phasing out nuclear and fossil fuels.
reception_impact: Provoked discussions and debate within both environmental and energy policy circles
Praised for its clarity, courage, and technical accessibility
Criticized by some clean energy advocates for downplaying renewables’ potential
Contributed to renewed interest in nuclear power among policymakers and the public
comparable_titles: Apocalypse Never: Why Environmental Alarmism Hurts Us All by Michael Shellenberger
A Bright Future: How Some Countries Have Solved Climate Change and the Rest Can Follow by Joshua S. Goldstein and Staffan A. Qvist
The Moral Case for Fossil Fuels by Alex Epstein
